rationale: C15 plausibly supplied a material rhetorical template: it grounds human equality in the Founding Fathers and the Declaration of Independence, describes national progress toward that ideal, and closes by urging continued progress. The child follows the same sequence while adapting it to school integration and public education. C12 has closely related religious and equality language, but its sequence is less similar. C14 overlaps materially on education and progress but lacks the child's distinctive equality-and-Declaration framework.

shared_material.child_excerpt: our forefathers enshrined this belief in the Declaration of Independence as a self-evident truth
shared_material.parent_excerpt: The ardent belief of our Founding Fathers in human dignity and freedom--enduringly expressed in the Declaration of Independence
shared_material.explanation: Both invoke the Founders and the Declaration as the authoritative source of the national ideal of human equality.

shared_material.child_excerpt: we constantly strive to achieve this ideal of the equality of man. We had been making progress--substantial progress--toward that goal.
shared_material.parent_excerpt: Americans can be proud of the progress made toward realization of this ideal of brotherhood
shared_material.explanation: The child closely reproduces the framing of equality or brotherhood as an ideal toward which the nation has made progress.

shared_material.child_excerpt: I fervently hope that soon the schools will reopen and that progress toward our goal will resume.
shared_material.parent_excerpt: Through such efforts as yours this progress will continue toward an America increasingly worthy of those ... dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.
shared_material.explanation: Both conclude with a forward-looking appeal for continued progress toward the founding ideal of equality.
